records.author: @whitedragem
records.text:
I would seek out the best brand, then their better lineups, and then buy the one with the LEAST features at the highest price.
This is based on decades of buying reference screens.
Littlest model in the flagship lineup from brands like Sony/Panasonic (TVs), or, and its hard to qualify modern PC monitors, but brand preferences like Asus look after customers/'consumers' well.

regarding OLED/'modern screens'; great ones make 30frames per second sources perfectly fine, even without picture processing engaged (latencies added, "soap opera effect" etc).

monitors do outpunch TVs, generally speaking,.. but everything by PRICEPOINT.
(you get what you pay for);
my advice is look for the best rated product with the biggest discount you can find in your local market.

If it isnt for 'desktop productivity' (first/foremost), then a slightly older OLED (rgb layout less than ideal for text), might prove a great bargain.
I saw a few Philips ultrawides at 60% off, and they included Philips ambilight which was based on commissioned research for cinema industry; Philips ambilight is good enough to buy one of THEIR products (true), but can be added (at big $ addition) to some other screens (eg some Samsung TVs allow running a Philips light control system/'ambilight').

I love power over USB input to monitors, and a 65watt margin would be my target.
as for screen update rate? anything above 120hz (to 165hz) (assuming OLEDs) is pretty top tier value to performance..

just know in the brightness war and cost war, a lot has gone downhill for OLED over the last decade.
Marketing insists things keep improving, but there is a LOT of half truths regarding this..

I moved on from the Lenovo (still beside my bed, not turned on for three months!) due to a budget Samsung 'the frame' being a vastly better fit for my needs. (it replaced my Panasonic reference OLED!)

Marketing/'reviews' sell stuff.
Always NEW stuff..
which means last years products need be talked down or new bullet point features heavily talked up..
Nothing gets around 'you get what you pay for'..
(second hand Sony flagships are ALWAYS great buys!!)

Motion resolution matters massively for media consumption (/gaming), yet is costly to implement and has generally slipped/downgraded when prices come down.
to this end, spec sheets are manipulative rather than truly informative..
eg the colour capability of my 'budget' sammy LCD TV when doing high brightness HDR is unseen by most OLED screens.
Samsung the frame is great in lit room, but low quality screen when considered in 'total darkness'.
OLED refresh rate greater than LCDs (120hz OLED a better choice than 240hz LCDs etc), but OLEDs generally are built for black environments..
eg Why my Lenovo is unused for three months (windows on all four walls AND daytime usage)

Consider YOUR needs and find reviewers matching those end goals!
cheers

records.author: @whitedragem
records.text:
apols I just gave a large response covering this.. won't rewrite 70% of it.

I moved on due to needing a daytime/'lit environment' screen.
30frames per second handling (poor) and no power delivery USB picture input would weigh heavy on my evaluation list.

30 frames per second handling is a great tell regarding picture processing for any set.. I have had recent reference LCD monitors that do poorly (not just an OLED issue!), and I have seen too tier Sony and Panasonic screens render 30fps input perfectly. (makes samsung and lg seem like junk!)

30 fps handling IS important, and most reviewers will just turn on tv picture processing or make out like high framerate input is necessary for OLEDs etc.
Their isnt any one screen that hands down beats all others, so VERY IMPORTANT to come up with your needs list.. (eg room lighting/hours of useage, sources to be considered, HDR vs SDR watch times/'weighting')
